sections.heading: Preparation timeline: a step-by-step checklist
sections.body:
Splitting the preparations into stages makes it easier on the owner and allows for the pet's behavioural adjustment: a cat needs a few days to get used to a large new object in the room, and pheromones need time to create a calm background.

## 1–2 weeks before the holidays
• Check windows and balconies: fit metal cat-proof screens with sturdy metal fastenings, and protective combs or side grilles on tilt-open windows.
• Prepare and check the cat's first-aid kit, replace anything past its expiry date.
• Save in your phone and put up somewhere visible the numbers of your own vet and the nearest 24-hour clinic.
• If your cat tends to be anxious, switch on a pheromone diffuser in advance in the room where the pet spends most of its time, and do whatever calms your cat.
• Prepare a safe alternative for climbing: a tall cat tree or a cardboard house that can stand next to the future Christmas tree as an alternative.

## 3–4 days before decorating: putting up the tree
• Choose an open spot (ideally in a corner) at a safe distance from sofas, wardrobes, tables and windowsills, so the cat can't jump into the middle of the branches.
• Assemble the bare tree and fix it firmly in a heavy stand, with extra anchoring to the wall or ceiling.
• Leave the tree completely bare for at least 3 days so the cat can explore it and lose its first interest before any decorations appear.
• Hide and protect all light cables and extension leads in rigid plastic trunking, or fix them along the skirting board.
• Keep an eye on your cat's interest in the tree. Running about and lying under the tree is perfectly normal. If the cat tries to climb the tree, you can try fixing it to the wall or something solid. It's important not to reinforce the cat's interest in the tree with your own behaviour (playing with it or even scolding it).

## The holiday night
• Put gift bags, ribbons and boxes of food away in a closed cupboard until it's time to hand them out.
• Don't leave festive dishes with mayonnaise, bones, onion, chocolate or alcohol unattended. Remember that a number of foods are off-limits for cats because they are dangerous to their health.
• Ask guests not to feed the cat from the table, to watch the front door and to put their bags and medicines away in closed cupboards.
• Before the fireworks start and before dark, close the windows, outer doors and cat flaps, draw the curtains tightly against the flashes and put on the TV, the radio or calm music in the background to cover the street noise with gentler sounds.
• Take out rubbish with bones, foil and ribbons promptly, to closed bins or out of the flat.

## The morning check after the party
• Vacuum the floor around the tree to pick up fallen natural or plastic needles.
• Check the light cables and the lower decorations for bite marks or damage.
• Clear away leftover festive food, burnt-out sparklers, sweet wrappers and foil out of the cat's reach.

sections.heading: The Christmas tree at home: choosing it, securing it and correcting the cat's behaviour
sections.body:
## Real or artificial tree: comparing the risks
What matters most is not what the tree is made of but how stable it is, how the water is protected and which decorations you choose. Each kind of tree has its own particular hazards.
• Water in the stand. A real tree (spruce, pine, fir) needs watering every day; bacteria and mould grow in an open bowl, and added fertiliser and especially aspirin are dangerous. An artificial tree (PVC or moulded needles) needs no water. In practice: put only clean water in a real tree's stand and close off access to the bowl tightly.
• Needles and resin. A real tree's sharp needles irritate the mouth and the digestive tract, in large amounts can block or perforate the gut, and cats are also sensitive to the essential oils in the needles. An artificial tree has no oils, but chewed plastic also irritates the digestive tract and, if swallowed, can cause a blockage. In practice: vacuum the floor under any tree, and if your cat likes to chew branches, a good artificial tree is the better choice.
• Risk of toppling. Both kinds carry a high risk without anchoring, and light artificial models fall over more easily. In practice: a heavy stand and anchoring to the wall or ceiling are a must.

## Securing the tree and protecting the stand, step by step
Jumping onto a poorly secured tree, a cat can bring it down on itself and get not only cuts from broken decorations but serious blunt injuries to the chest or belly, including a ruptured lung, a ruptured spleen and bruised liver or kidneys.
The tree is set up and anchored strictly before any decorations go on.
• Put the trunk in the heaviest, widest stand you can get, built to take the jolt of a cat jumping.
• You can tie the upper third of the trunk with strong fishing line, cord or thin cable to a ceiling hook or to an anchor ring screwed into the wall (tip: drill the hole behind a picture you take down first, so you can hang it back after the holidays).
• For extra stability, add a second fixing low on the trunk, securing the tree at the skirting board.
• For a real tree, use only clean water with no preservatives or substances dangerous to the cat.
• Cover the water reservoir with a tight-fitting lid, a fine mesh, a rigid tree collar or a tightly fastened tree skirt, leaving a way to top up the water every day.
• Don't put the cat's own toys and treats under the branches, especially anything with catnip.

## Decorations, lights and cables
The most dangerous Christmas decorations for cats are tinsel, tinsel garlands, streamers and long gift ribbons. The shiny, rustling strips tempt a cat to play, one end easily catches on the little barbs at the root of the tongue, and the rest gets swallowed.
The gut's movements pull the thread tight and literally gather the loops of intestine like an accordion, which cuts through the wall, causes peritonitis and calls for emergency abdominal surgery. The only reliable protection is to keep tinsel, tinsel garlands and long ribbons out of the house altogether. If this happens, see a vet urgently.
Fragile glass and ceramic baubles break into sharp shards when they fall, injuring paws, mouth and digestive tract. Salt-dough ornaments are especially dangerous: even when completely dry, eating them can cause a severe, life-threatening electrolyte imbalance. It's best to leave the lower branches bare or decorate them with large unbreakable items of wood, fabric or impact-resistant plastic, hung not on S-shaped wire hooks (these are easy to swallow) but on fabric loops or rings closed with pliers. For lighting, choose low-voltage LED lights with a steady, non-flickering glow, hide the cable to the socket in a plastic protective cover, and always switch the lights off when you go out or go to bed.

## Barriers, deterrents and positive redirection: what works and what does harm
The most lasting change in behaviour comes from combining physical barriers, unpleasant surfaces to touch and an attractive alternative next to the tree. Remember that a cat most likely goes for the tree simply out of curiosity.
Around the base of the trunk, put a rigid collar, a low pen-style fence (as a barrier that slows the cat down), sheets of foil, a plastic mat with the spikes facing up, or strips of double-sided tape on mats.
A tall scratching post or cat tree can stand nearby; reward the cat with treats and play for choosing the allowed spot.
At the same time, a number of popular tips from the internet are harmful or dangerous.
A water spray bottle and any deterrents that cause pain are not recommended: water only teaches the cat to climb the tree when the owner is away, undermines its trust in people and can trigger redirected aggression towards other pets.
Automatic compressed-air cans with a motion sensor get mixed reviews: some owners find them effective, but animal welfare organisations (PAWS in particular) warn that the sudden hiss can badly frighten an anxious cat and also goes off for children and guests. Finally, despite some blogs advising you to spray the branches with lemon juice or rub them with menthol ointments, veterinary toxicologists (ASPCA, Pet Poison Helpline) warn that the essential oils of citrus, mint and pine are toxic to cats. If you want to use a deterring citrus smell, the only acceptable way is to put fresh peel in thick breathable pouches deep inside the tree, so that paws and tongue never touch the oil.

sections.heading: Dangerous spots and hidden threats in your home
sections.body:
## Windows on tilt: a deadly plastic trap
While cooking for the holidays and when guests arrive, windows are often left tilted open. The cat's head and body pass easily through the wide upper part of the opening; then, trying to get out or while playing, the animal slides down into the narrow gap and gets stuck fast. Pressure on the neck quickly leads to asphyxia, and being trapped at the belly squeezes large blood vessels, including the abdominal aorta, cutting off blood to the back of the body and causing serious injuries to the spine and legs as the cat struggles to free itself.
Leaving windows tilted open without protective side grilles or child restrictors is unacceptable, and ordinary insect screens won't hold a cat's weight - they need to be replaced with metal cat-proof screens.

## Holiday plants and bouquets
Gift bouquets in December are often a far greater threat than the tree itself. Keep in mind that a «non-toxic» label in databases such as the ASPCA's means there is no systemic poison, but eating a large amount of any plant material can still upset the stomach and cause vomiting. See the list of important plants in the section about plants.

## The festive table, guests and rubbish
Festive food is one of the reasons vet clinics get so many visits over the holidays. Salads with mayonnaise dressing (Olivier salad, «herring under a fur coat»), marinades, sausages, ham, fried and smoked meat are loaded with fat, salt and spices and easily cause gastritis or acute pancreatitis. Veterinary guides to the holiday table don't single out red and black caviar, but any very salty and fatty delicacies are generally undesirable for cats because of the strain on the digestive tract and the kidneys.
Dangerous and toxic foods that must not be left within the cat's reach include:
• Cooked poultry and fish bones (they splinter into sharp fragments that can injure the oesophagus and the intestinal wall).
• Onion, garlic, leek and chives, including in gravies and minced meat (they destroy red blood cells and cause anaemia).
• Grapes and raisins (they cause toxic damage to the kidneys).
• Chocolate and cocoa (they contain theobromine), as well as sugar-free sweets and chewing gum with xylitol (general guidance for pets notes the risk of a sharp drop in blood sugar within 30 minutes and of liver damage).
• Alcohol and dishes containing alcohol, including drops of champagne (toxic even in tiny doses).
• Raw yeast dough, aluminium foil from roasting, and citrus fruit, including tangerines (they irritate the stomach and cause allergic reactions).

## Hidden chemical and household traps: batteries, snow globes, aroma diffusers and sparklers
Holiday decorations include a number of items whose danger isn't obvious at first sight.
• Lithium coin batteries (3 V). Found in remote controls for lights, LED candles, greeting cards and key rings. Lodged in the oesophagus, even an intact battery conducts current and causes a deep burn.
Prevention: use only screw-fastened battery compartments and change batteries in a closed room.
• Cylindrical alkaline batteries (AA, AAA). Found in battery packs for lights, torches and toys. When bitten through, they leak corrosive alkali (potassium hydroxide), which causes liquefactive necrosis of the tissue; the first ulcers appear within 1–2 hours, and the burn reaches its full depth within up to 24 hours.
Prevention: keep battery packs out of reach and store spare batteries in sturdy boxes.
• Snow globes and artificial snow. Used as souvenir globes, and as sprays and powders for decorating. The liquid in glass snow globes often contains sweet-tasting ethylene glycol (antifreeze), which causes fatal kidney poisoning, and dry artificial snow powder swells when wet and can block the gut.
Prevention: keep souvenirs in closed display cabinets and don't use artificial snow on the tree.
• Essential oils, liquid potpourri and candles. The sources of risk are active (ultrasonic) diffusers, oil burners and candles.
Prevention: replace open candles and room fragrance with unscented LED candles (if you do use a diffuser, choose safe blends, run it briefly in a room the cat can't get into and air the room afterwards).
• Sparklers and fireworks. The danger comes from sparks indoors, burnt-out sparklers, ash and debris outside. They cause contact burns and irritate the airways with smoke; if firework compounds are swallowed, digestive upset and poisoning with barium salts or heavy metals are possible.
Prevention: don't light sparklers in the same room as the cat, and pick up the spent sticks straight away.

## Fireworks and the stress of guests
Holiday noise, bright flashes, rearranged furniture and strangers in the house take away the animal's usual sense of control over its territory.
How to help the cat differs between having guests over and fireworks outside on a quiet evening at home. If a noisy party with guests is planned, set up a separate «quiet room» for the cat in advance, with a bed, water, food, a scratching post and a litter box (it's better not to move the main litter box from its usual place for the holiday), and ask guests not to go in there and not to force contact on the animal.
If no guests are coming but fireworks are booming outside, it can help not to shut the cat in one room if it usually moves freely around the home - closed doors can themselves add to its anxiety. Instead, lock all outer doors, windows and cat flaps, draw thick curtains, put on the TV or calm music to mask the bangs, and give the cat free access to its usual hiding places (boxes with blankets, the space under the bed, the top shelves of wardrobes).
A pet that has hidden must not be pulled out of its hiding place or picked up by force to be comforted - it's better to stay calm, behave as usual and wait for the cat to come out on its own.

sections.heading: SOS protocol: first aid, red flags and the cat's first-aid kit
sections.body:
## Critical don'ts: what is deadly dangerous to do at home
• Never give a cat 3% hydrogen peroxide to make it vomit. Unlike in dogs, it doesn't work reliably in cats but causes severe necrotising ulcerative gastritis, oxygen embolism of the blood vessels, inhaled foam and acute pulmonary oedema. Seek help from a vet.
• Never pull on tinsel, thread or ribbon hanging out of the mouth or the anus. Pulling works like a saw and is very likely to cut through the intestinal wall, causing peritonitis. Seek help from a vet.
• Don't touch the cat if it is still biting a cable or lying on a live wire. First pull the plug out of the socket or switch off the power at the fuse box. Seek help from a vet.
• Don't make the cat vomit if it has swallowed bones, batteries, corrosive liquids or petroleum products. Fragments or alkali coming back up injure the oesophagus and airways a second time. Seek help from a vet.
• Don't use human painkillers (aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen) or antibiotic ointments such as Neosporin. Seek help from a vet.
